newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: High rates, OECD keep Slovak BSE bulls running.
newsitem.headline: High rates, OECD keep Slovak BSE bulls running.

text.p: High interest rates and potential membership in the OECD continue to fuel bullish sentiment on the Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE), despite a slowdown at many other bourses in the region.

Brokers said on Thursday the BSE, the smallest of eastern Europe's four leading bourses with capitalisation of $2.5 billion, has finally caught the eyes of foreign investors, who are helping push the SAX index to fresh highs for the year almost daily.

"Many foreign investors are (now) interested in Slovak shares in anticipation of the country soon being accepted to the OECD and these new circumstances will equalise their prices with similar issues abroad," Vladimir Kuklis, an market analyst at bank CSOB, told Reuters.
The index closed on Wednesday at 205.58, its third year-high in the past four BSE sessions.
Other market's in the region such as Warsaw, Budapest and Prague have posted strong gains since the start of the year, but have tailed off recently.

The BSE has lagged behind because of complaints over a lack of market transparency and low liquidity. But analysts said membership of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) should help allay some fears by forcing tighter market regulation.

The renewed interest has picked up recently, boosting overall turnover on the bourse markedly with February posting a record monthly volume of 17.1 billion crowns ($511 million), up from 10.5 billion in January.

Analysts said most issues that are comparable with similar stocks in neighbouring countries -- such as oil refiner Slovnaft and steel maker VSZ -- have drawn investors who consider them undervalued against their regional competitors.
This, coupled with a rise in interest rates since the beginning of the year were enough to trigger the spending spree.

"One must keep in his mind that Slovakia lays a bit out of the main road for the foreign capital at the moment," Libor Briska of Creditanstalt said. "It attracts the investors only by single events, not constantly."

Slovak interbank money rates jumped to record levels above 25 percent in the first weeks of January after the central bank moved to rein in a rapidly growing money supply and cool off a consumption-led domestic credit boom.

Although the bourse's fortunes have appeared to turn the corner for the time being, traders said long-standing liquidity problems remain one of the BSE's most serious troubles, with many investors unable to buy larger parcels of the shares they want.
The overall free-flow of share capital traded on the BSE totals only $900 million, against some $5 billion on the Prague bourse, $4.6 billion in Warsaw and $3.5 billion in Budapest, Briska said.
The market also suffers from a lack of new issues and a weak interest among domestic investors.
"Strategic stakes in medium and small companies have been mostly already placed, leaving these issues uninteresting for long-term investors," Briska said.
"I consider this low liquidity, along with the country's less-than-good political image as the main barriers for a long-term improvement."
